Let's talk about what's happening on your BNR-1 transformer — the full picture, in plain terms. This transformer served your facility every operating day through May 2026, and the data tells a clear story. Across 44,640 minutes of recorded operation, BNR-1 averaged 1,500 kilovolt-amperes of apparent power, with regular peaks reaching 1,587.5 kVA. Your average real power — the work actually getting done — was 1,346.8 kilowatts. The gap between those two numbers is your reactive drag, and it's substantial. Your power factor on BNR-1 is averaging 89.77 percent. That means for every 10 dollars of electrical capacity flowing through this transformer, roughly one dollar is circulating back and forth doing nothing productive — just generating heat. That reactive obligation averages 635.9 kilovolt-amperes reactive, and it peaked at over 1,000 kVAR in May. That's the number that determines how we size a correction system — and it tells us you need three H490 MPTS units to cover this transformer's worst-case reactive demand. Now add the voltage picture. Those dips are happening roughly every six to eight days. For your motors, drives, and compressors, that's repeated undervoltage stress — and in an untuned field, that stress isn't being mitigated. It accumulates. The BT analysis estimates your total annual waste at approximately $425,000 — reactive losses, thermal burden, and cooling overhead combined. Your cooling system alone is spending an estimated $144,000 per year just managing the waste heat this transformer produces. Three H490 units, at a planning-level installed estimate of approximately $600,000, would lift your power factor to 99.5 percent and recover the overwhelming majority of that waste. That's the opportunity on BNR-1, and it's well-defined. ---

The CSV is ground truth here.

The overall field condition for BNR-1 in May 2026 is: **high utilization, chronically low power factor, elevated and variable reactive demand, persistent undervoltage, and an untuned field that is generating waste and heat every operating hour without correction.** This is a transformer that needs an engineering response — not someday, but on a defined schedule.

BNR1.voltage_stability_findings:
**BNR-1 Voltage Health | May 2026 | Untuned**

The voltage field on BNR-1 is running compressed and chronically depressed. The CSV confirms an average line-to-neutral voltage of 273.85 volts — which converts to approximately 474.4 volts line-to-line. Nominal for this class of industrial installation is 480 volts line-to-line. That places BNR-1's average voltage at roughly 1.2 percent below nominal even at the long-run average, and the V-view image makes clear this isn't a transient condition — it's the steady-state operating environment for this transformer.

Beyond the chronic suppression, the V view identifies five discrete triangular voltage-dip events across the month, annotated at 458.4V, 459.6V, 456.8V, 460.7V, and 457V — all occurring during what appear to be production cycle transitions, spaced roughly six to eight days apart. The floor of these events is 456.8 volts line-to-line, which is 23.2 volts below the 480V nominal — a 4.8 percent undervoltage excursion. These are not momentary flickers. Each triangular dip event represents a sustained load transition that depresses the voltage envelope for a measurable interval.

Two gold vertical streaks were identified in the BT chart body — one near May 8th and one near May 19th through 20th — consistent with power interruption events. Each streak is estimated at approximately 60 to 90 minutes at 1-minute resolution, for a combined estimated outage duration of roughly 120 to 180 minutes across the month. These outage intervals align precisely with the voltage-dip annotations in the V view, suggesting the two events are correlated — either planned load interruptions or unplanned outages that also manifested as voltage disturbances on recovery.

The device-health risk here is high. BNR-1 feeds heavy motor loads in a food processing environment — compressors, conveyors, refrigeration systems, and rendering equipment. Every percent of sustained undervoltage adds disproportionate thermal stress to motor windings, reduces torque margins, increases slip in induction motors, and shortens the service life of drives and contactors. A field running 1.2 percent below nominal on average, with dip events reaching 4.8 percent below nominal, and carrying an average reactive load of 635.9 kVAR simultaneously — that is a conditions-for-failure environment. It's not a warning sign to monitor. It's an active stress state to correct.

BNR1.reactive_harmonic_findings:
**BNR-1 Reactive and Harmonic Profile | May 2026 | Untuned**

The reactive burden on BNR-1 is structural, not episodic. The CSV confirms a 635.9 kVAR monthly average, which means at any given moment during production operations, this transformer is obligated to circulate approximately 636 kilovolt-amperes reactive — energy that travels back and forth through the windings without performing useful work, generating heat with every cycle. The BT header independently reads 659 kVAR average, and the M view's live reactive annotation hits 673 kVAR during peak production — all consistent with a field that never sheds its reactive obligation under load.

The critical number, however, is the CSV-estimated kVAR MAX of 1,017 kVAR. That is the peak reactive demand BNR-1 imposed on the electrical infrastructure during May. It's nearly 60 percent above the monthly average, and it's substantially higher than the 725 kVAR figure shown in the BT image header — a discrepancy that exceeded the 10 percent cross-check threshold and triggered a flag. The CSV wins. 1,017 kVAR is the sizing anchor for any correction system deployed here.

On the harmonic side, the M view confirms a current total harmonic distortion average of 6.2 percent iTHD, with a peak of 10.8 percent iTHD. That gap between average and peak — nearly double the baseline at the worst moments — is a signature of switching load events. Variable-frequency drives, soft starters, and rectifier-based loads cycling through production states are the most likely sources. At a food processing facility of this scale, these loads are unavoidable, but their harmonic contribution is continuously aging the transformer insulation, adding to core losses, and contributing to the thermal burden even during periods when the kVA loading itself looks moderate.

The amperage trace in the M view ran a persistent band with a peak annotation of 1,930.6 amps, and the BT header confirms a max amperage of 2,067.7 amps — telling you this transformer is seeing full-load current conditions regularly throughout the production cycle. The combined effect of reactive drag, harmonic distortion, and high-current loading is a thermally stressed transformer operating without correction.

BNR1.operational_stress_interpretation:
**BNR-1 Operational Stress | May 2026 | Untuned**

Pull back and look at what all of these signals mean together for a facility like Foster Farms Livingston HQ. BNR-1 is not a transformer running casually under light industrial loads. It's a production workhorse — the BT chart shows kVA supply at or above the 1,587.5 kVA planning target for the overwhelming majority of weekday operating hours across approximately 21 to 22 working days in May. This facility is running at high duty cycle, and BNR-1 is carrying that full operational burden continuously.

Now layer on the stress profile. The power factor is 89.77 percent — not terrible by some industrial standards, but at this load level and transformer size, that 10.23 percent reactive fraction translates to hundreds of kVAR of circulating reactive current, all of it generating heat without generating output. The BT header estimates a thermal burden of 568,608 BTU per hour with cooling costs of approximately $16.48 per hour — that's roughly $144,000 per year just to manage the waste heat this transformer is producing. And because the field is untuned, that thermal burden is not being reduced between billing periods. It accumulates.

The two power interruption events — estimated at 60 to 90 minutes each, for a combined 2 to 3 hours of downtime in May — represent a real operational cost at a food processing facility where product temperature control, process continuity, and food safety timelines are not flexible. Even a 90-minute unplanned outage on a processing or cold storage line carries consequences that go well beyond the energy bill.

The voltage dip events clustering every six to eight days add another layer. Each dip to the 456–460V range is a stress test on every induction motor and power electronics component connected downstream. Variable-frequency drives operating through sustained undervoltage cycles will see elevated DC bus stress and increased fault rates over time. Contactor coils and motor starters rated for 480V nominal are being energized at 4 to 5 percent below their design point — repeatedly, month after month. In an untuned field with no correction in place, these stress cycles accumulate silently until something fails.

The aggregate picture for BNR-1 in May 2026 is a transformer under sustained multi-axis stress: high reactive burden, elevated harmonic content, chronic undervoltage, high utilization, and two documented power interruptions — all without any active correction system. This is the operational profile that, left unaddressed, produces accelerating equipment degradation and rising maintenance costs in the months ahead.

The field holds at 99.5 percent PF continuously, minimum to maximum, which means the correction isn't just effective at average load — it's holding the line during peak events too.

The thermal burden drops dramatically — the BT header pegged thermal waste at 568,608 BTU per hour, and with reactive current largely eliminated, transformer winding temperatures decrease, cooling system run-time shortens, and the estimated $144,000 per year in cooling overhead begins to recover. The voltage environment also stabilizes — reactive compensation reduces the inductive voltage drop that is partly responsible for BNR-1's chronic undervoltage condition, giving motors and drives a healthier supply voltage to work against. The 2,067.7-amp peak current draw decreases as apparent power demand falls with improved power factor, reducing I²R losses in the conductors and transformer windings proportionally.

The BT header estimated total waste of approximately $425,113 per year. The S view represents the majority of that waste being recovered annually. In an untuned field where efficiency is drifting downward and heat burden tends to rise month over month without correction, the simulated MPTS outcome defines the gap between the facility's current trajectory and where it could be operating with tuning assigned.

BNR1.recommended_engineering_attention_areas:
**BNR-1 Engineering Priorities | May 2026**

Based on the full May 2026 analysis of BNR-1 at Foster Farms Livingston HQ, the following engineering attention areas are recommended in priority order.

**First — Reactive compensation deployment.** Three H490 units sized to the 1,017 kVAR CSV-confirmed peak. This is the highest-leverage single action available for BNR-1. Every month without correction is another month of avoidable thermal burden, reactive energy waste, and accelerating insulation aging on a transformer already running at high utilization. The planning-level investment of approximately $600,000 installed should be evaluated against the estimated $425,000-plus annual waste cost confirmed by the BT analysis.

**Second — Voltage baseline investigation.** The chronic 1.2 percent average undervoltage and the recurring 4.8 percent dip events every six to eight days warrant a dedicated voltage survey. Engineering should confirm whether the BNR-1 supply tap position is optimized, whether transformer on-load tap changer settings (if equipped) can be adjusted, and whether reactive compensation deployment itself will partially correct the voltage suppression by reducing the inductive voltage drop in the supply circuit.

**Third — Outage root-cause review.** Two power interruption events totaling approximately 2 to 3 hours of estimated downtime were identified in May. At a food processing facility, outage events of that duration during production hours carry food safety, product loss, and regulatory implications. Engineering should confirm whether these were planned maintenance windows, protective relay operations, or unplanned supply disturbances, and whether any upstream protective coordination improvements are warranted.

**Fourth — Harmonic survey and mitigation assessment.** The 10.8 percent iTHD peak, occurring at nearly double the 6.2 percent average, indicates load-switching harmonic events that are contributing to transformer core heating and conductor losses. A dedicated harmonic survey during peak production transitions is recommended to identify the primary source loads — likely VFD-driven equipment — and evaluate whether passive or active harmonic filtering should be incorporated into the correction scope alongside reactive compensation.

**Fifth — Tuning assignment and monthly trend monitoring.** As an untuned field, BNR-1's efficiency will continue to drift downward and heat burden will tend to rise month over month without a correction assignment. Establishing a baseline Mercury trend cadence and assigning a tuning target are essential for tracking whether field conditions are stable, improving, or deteriorating between the current analysis period and correction deployment.

In an untuned field, power factor can sit anywhere from the low 80s to the mid-90s, depending on load mix and field age. The gap between those numbers — say, 85 percent and 99.5 percent — represents reactive current that is generating heat, stressing insulation, and showing up on your utility bill. That heat accumulates in BTU per hour. In warm ambient environments — think summer months, enclosed transformer rooms, facilities running high-density refrigeration — that thermal burden is compounded by the ambient temperature. Transformer insulation ages faster under elevated temperature. The relationship is well established: every 10 degrees Celsius of sustained excess temperature roughly halves the effective insulation lifespan. That's not a small effect. That's a direct capital asset risk. Now, for AGENTICTEA specifically, I have to tell you that neither the CSV data from our Mercury analysis nor the image captures from the baseline-target, voltage, monthly, and savings views were available for this analysis. Every numeric anchor — peak demand in kilowatts, reactive average and kVAR maximum, power factor percentage, energy waste in dollars per year, thermal burden in BTU per hour, cooling overhead in dollars per hour — all return as value unavailable. That means I cannot complete the H490 unit count calculation. The sizing rule is straightforward: take the kVAR maximum, divide by four hundred, and round up. But without a confirmed kVAR maximum, that calculation stays open. I cannot project the annual savings recovery. I cannot confirm the payback timeline. And I cannot confirm whether any outage events were present in the capture period — gold streak detection in the chart image returns as unconfirmed. What I can do is frame the correction case structurally, so that when data is resubmitted, this analysis populates immediately. The planning install estimate for one H490 unit is approximately $200,000 installed. That is a planning-level estimate — it is not a binding quote, and final pricing will depend on engineering scope, site access, and installation complexity. In comparable untuned industrial fields where reactive demand runs in the range of 200 to 400 kVAR, annual energy waste and thermal burden costs frequently run into five to six figures annually. MPTS correction at 99.5 percent power factor typically recovers the majority of that waste, bringing the transformer into an efficient, thermally stable operating state. The voltage health picture for AGENTICTEA is similarly incomplete. Without the V image, we cannot confirm whether voltage dip events are present, how frequently they occur, or how deep they run relative to the 480-volt line-to-line nominal. In facilities with heavy inductive switching loads, repeated voltage dips below nominal are a real device stress factor — they strain motor windings at every start, and they accumulate into measurable insulation degradation over operating months. My recommendation is direct: resubmit the BT, V, M, and S image captures alongside the Mercury CSV for AGENTICTEA. Once that data is in, we complete the reactive baseline, confirm the unit count, build the savings projection, and bring this transformer into the full group site overview with real numbers. Right now, AGENTICTEA is the data gap in an otherwise structured analysis. The untuned condition continues until correction is assigned. Every month that passes is another month of reactive loss, thermal accumulation, and compounding cost. That's the nature of an uncorrected field — and it's exactly the condition MPTS is built to stop. That's electromagnetic stewardship — and that's the Unity standard.
